title: Parallel-Axis Theorem
short_intro: The parallel-axis theorem states that the moment of inertia of a rigid body about any arbitrary axis is equal to the moment of inertia about a parallel axis passing through its centre of mass plus the product of the mass of the body and the square of the perpendicular distance between the two axes. It applies to any rigid body regardless of its geometry or planar symmetry.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Direct numerical calculations using I = I<sub>cm</sub> + Md<sup>2</sup> for standard uniform bodies such as rods, rings, discs, and spheres about parallel axes.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Advanced applications involving composite bodies, continuous mass distributions with variable linear or areal density, and tensor-based rotational dynamics.

prerequisites: Definition of Moment of Inertia and Radius of Gyration
Properties and coordinate determination of Centre of Mass
Integration techniques and vector summation in rigid body dynamics

concept_notes.heading: Statement of Parallel-Axis Theorem
bullets: The theorem relates the moment of inertia I about an axis to the moment of inertia I<sub>cm</sub> about a parallel axis passing through the centre of mass.
Mathematical expression: I = I<sub>cm</sub> + Md<sup>2</sup>, where M is the total mass of the body and d is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel axes.
Both axes must remain strictly parallel to each other for the theorem to hold true.

concept_notes.heading: Condition of Applicability
bullets: One of the two axes of rotation must necessarily pass through the centre of mass of the rigid body.
The theorem is valid for both two-dimensional (planar) and three-dimensional (solid) rigid bodies of any arbitrary shape.
It holds for continuous mass distributions as well as discrete systems of particles.

concept_notes.heading: Physical Interpretation
bullets: The moment of inertia is minimum about an axis passing through the centre of mass compared to any other parallel axis.
Shifting the axis away from the centre of mass always increases the moment of inertia by the additive term Md<sup>2</sup>.
The term Md<sup>2</sup> represents the rotational inertia contributed by treating the entire mass concentrated at the centre of mass combined with the displaced axis.

concept_notes.heading: Significance in Rotational Dynamics
bullets: Simplifies complex moment of inertia calculations by reducing them to standard centre of mass values.
Essential for analyzing compound pendulums and bodies rotating about a fixed hinge or pivot that does not coincide with the centre of mass.
Used alongside the perpendicular-axis theorem to determine moments of inertia for complex three-dimensional geometries.

derivations.title: Derivation of Parallel-Axis Theorem for a Continuous Body
derivations.conditions: Rigid body of mass M, axis passing through CM, and a parallel axis at distance d.
steps: Let an axis pass through the centre of mass C along the z-axis. Consider a mass element dm located at position vector r = (x, y, z) relative to C.
The moment of inertia about the axis passing through the centre of mass is given by I_{cm} = \int (x^2 + y^2) dm.
Consider a parallel axis at a perpendicular distance d along the x-axis. The distance squared of the mass element dm from this new axis is given by ((x + d)^2 + y^2).
The moment of inertia about the new axis is I = \int ((x + d)^2 + y^2) dm = \int (x^2 + y^2 + 2dx + d^2) dm.
Expanding the integral: I = \int (x^2 + y^2) dm + 2d \int x dm + d^2 \int dm.
By definition of the centre of mass relative to the origin at CM, the term \int x dm = 0. Also, \int dm = M and \int (x^2 + y^2) dm = I_{cm}.
Substituting these yields the final relation: I = I_{cm} + Md^2.

formula_sheet.name: Parallel-Axis Theorem
formula_sheet.variables: I = Moment of inertia about new axis, I_{cm} = Moment of inertia about parallel axis through CM, M = Total mass, d = Perpendicular distance
formula_sheet.conditions: One axis must pass through the centre of mass and both axes must be parallel.

formula_sheet.name: Moment of Inertia of Uniform Rod (about CM)
formula_sheet.variables: M = Mass of rod, L = Length of rod
formula_sheet.conditions: Axis perpendicular to rod passing through its midpoint.

formula_sheet.name: Moment of Inertia of Uniform Rod (about End)
formula_sheet.variables: M = Mass of rod, L = Length of rod
formula_sheet.conditions: Axis perpendicular to rod passing through one end (derived using d = L/2).

formula_sheet.name: Moment of Inertia of Circular Ring (about Tangent in Plane)
formula_sheet.variables: M = Mass of ring, R = Radius of ring
formula_sheet.conditions: Axis in the plane of the ring and tangent to its circumference (I_{cm} = 1/2 MR^2, d = R).

formula_sheet.name: Moment of Inertia of Circular Disc (about Tangent in Plane)
formula_sheet.variables: M = Mass of disc, R = Radius of disc
formula_sheet.conditions: Axis in the plane of the disc and tangent to its edge (I_{cm} = 1/4 MR^2, d = R).

formula_sheet.name: Moment of Inertia of Circular Disc (about Tangent Perpendicular to Plane)
formula_sheet.variables: M = Mass of disc, R = Radius of disc
formula_sheet.conditions: Axis perpendicular to the plane of the disc passing through its edge (I_{cm} = 1/2 MR^2, d = R).

formula_sheet.name: Moment of Inertia of Solid Sphere (about Tangent)
formula_sheet.variables: M = Mass of sphere, R = Radius of sphere
formula_sheet.conditions: Axis tangent to the surface of the solid sphere (I_{cm} = 2/5 MR^2, d = R).

formula_sheet.name: Moment of Inertia of Hollow Sphere (about Tangent)
formula_sheet.variables: M = Mass of solid/thin spherical shell, R = Radius
formula_sheet.conditions: Axis tangent to the surface of the thin spherical shell (I_{cm} = 2/3 MR^2, d = R).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Variation of Moment of Inertia with Axis Shift (Graph)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A parabolic curve plotting Moment of Inertia (I) on the y-axis against perpendicular distance (d) on the x-axis, with the minimum at I_{cm} when d = 0.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that the moment of inertia increases quadratically with distance d from the centre of mass axis according to I = I_{cm} + Md^2.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting graphical dependence of rotational inertia on axis position in objective questions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Torsional Pendulum Experiment
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup showing a rigid body suspended by a wire, rotated horizontally to measure time period T.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Allows experimental verification of moment of inertia and verification of parallel-axis theorem by adding symmetrical masses at known distances d.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Understanding laboratory verification methods for rotational mechanics parameters.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Compound Pendulum Oscillation Setup
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A rigid bar pivoted about an off-centre knife edge oscillating under gravity.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Time period T = 2*pi*sqrt(I / (M g l)), where I is evaluated using the parallel-axis theorem about the pivot point (I = I_{cm} + Ml^2).
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Solving numericals involving compound pendulum frequency and equivalent length.

solved_numericals.question: Find the moment of inertia of a uniform thin rod of mass 2 kg and length 1.0 m about an axis passing through one of its ends and perpendicular to its length.
solution_steps: Identify the formula for the moment of inertia of a rod about its centre of mass: I_{cm} = (1/12) M L^2.
Identify the distance d from the centre of mass to the end of the rod: d = L / 2 = 0.5 m.

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the moment of inertia of a circular disc of mass 4 kg and radius 0.5 m about a tangent lying in the plane of the disc.
solution_steps: The moment of inertia of a disc about its diameter (passing through CM in its plane) is I_{cm} = (1/4) M R^2.
The distance from the diameter to the tangent in the plane is equal to the radius: d = R = 0.5 m.
Apply the parallel-axis theorem: I = I_{cm} + M d^2 = 0.25 + 4 * (0.5)^2 = 0.25 + 4 * 0.25 = 0.25 + 1.0 = 1.25 kg m^2.

solved_numericals.question: A uniform square plate has mass M and side length a. Find its moment of inertia about an axis passing through one of its corners and perpendicular to the plane of the plate.
solution_steps: The moment of inertia of a square plate about an axis perpendicular to its plane through the centre of mass is given by I_{cm} = (1/6) M a^2 (derived using perpendicular-axis theorem with I_{xx} = I_{yy} = (1/12) M a^2).
The perpendicular distance d from the centre of the square to any corner is the half-diagonal: d = sqrt((a/2)^2 + (a/2)^2) = (a * sqrt(2)) / 2 = a / sqrt(2).
Apply the parallel-axis theorem: I = I_{cm} + M d^2 = (1/6) M a^2 + M (a^2 / 2) = M a^2 * (1/6 + 1/2) = M a^2 * (1/6 + 3/6) = (4/6) M a^2 = (2/3) M a^2.

assumptions_and_limitations: The theorem assumes the body is rigid, meaning the relative positions of mass elements do not change under rotation.
It is strictly required that the two axes under consideration are mutually parallel.
One of the axes must pass precisely through the centre of mass; the theorem cannot directly transfer inertia between two arbitrary non-CM parallel axes without an intermediate step via the CM.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Applying I = I_{cm} + Md^2 between any two parallel axes, even if neither passes through the centre of mass.
common_misconceptions.correct: One of the axes must pass through the centre of mass of the body.
common_misconceptions.why: The integral term \int x dm is only guaranteed to vanish when the origin of the coordinate system is located at the centre of mass.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Assuming the parallel-axis theorem only applies to two-dimensional planar objects.
common_misconceptions.correct: The theorem applies equally to all 1D, 2D, and 3D rigid bodies.
common_misconceptions.why: The derivation relies on spatial coordinates (x, y, z) and holds true for any continuous or discrete three-dimensional mass distribution.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Confusing the perpendicular distance d with the total distance along the body's surface.
common_misconceptions.correct: d must always be the perpendicular distance measured orthogonal to the direction of the parallel axes.
common_misconceptions.why: The shift in the moment of inertia depends strictly on the perpendicular separation between the lines of the axes of rotation.
